summary: Gives guidelines for designing congestion notification in lower-layer or tunnelling protocols that encapsulate IP. The aim is for explicit congestion signals to travel consistently into IP and up to the transport layer. It is a Best Current Practice and updates RFC 3819.

eli5.summary: When a road jams, signs should pass the word on. This tells designers of protocols that wrap IP to pass the congestion warning along.

questions: how to add ecn to a tunnel protocol
how should a tunnel egress handle ecn marks
subtitle: How to carry congestion signals across tunnels and lower-layer networks so they reach the IP layer and the transport protocol.

tldr.problem: When a lower-layer buffer or tunnel marks congestion instead of dropping a packet, that explicit signal is lost unless the layers above it are designed to pick it up and pass it on.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC splits lower layers into four modes (feed-forward-and-up, feed-up-and-forward, feed-backward and null) and gives guidelines for each, with detailed encapsulation and decapsulation rules for the first.
tldr.outcome: Designers who follow the guidelines get ECN signals that interwork across technologies, with IP acting as a portability layer. This is a Best Current Practice (BCP 89) that updates RFC 3819.

today: RFC 9599 is a Best Current Practice published in August 2024 that updates RFC 3819. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Congestion Signals Need Guidelines
sections.content:
Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) lets a congested queue mark a proportion of IP packets with the congestion experienced (CE) codepoint instead of dropping them. Given a suitable marking scheme, ECN removes nearly all congestion loss and cuts delay. When a lower-layer buffer drops a packet, the packet disappears from every layer. When it marks a frame header or the outer header of a tunnel, the mark has to be propagated explicitly up the layers.

Incremental deployment is the delicate part. If the device that strips the outer header does not pass the mark on, or the receiver cannot understand ECN, the signal is silently lost and congestion builds. In those cases congestion has to be shown by dropping the packet, not marking it.

The document only covers wire protocol processing of congestion notification. It makes no recommendations about marking or congestion response algorithms. It uses SHOULD more than MUST because each protocol design involves different compromises, but a design that skips a SHOULD MUST include a sound justification. It updates Section 13 of RFC 3819 by replacing its last two paragraphs with a single sentence that points here.
sections.eli5: If a warning sign is hidden behind a wall, nobody sees it. These rules make sure the warning gets passed along, and if it cannot be passed along safely, the packet is dropped instead.

sections.title: The Four Modes of Operation
sections.content:
The RFC groups lower layers by how congestion information moves.

  • Feed-forward-and-up: nodes feed congestion notification forward within the lower layer toward the egress, which then propagates it up into the forwarded IP header. The destination transport feeds it back to the source, for example in a TCP acknowledgement. IP-in-IP tunnels (RFC 6040) and MPLS (RFC 5129) already work this way.
  • Feed-up-and-forward: a lower-layer switch marks the IP header directly, wherever it is. An example is a Layer 3 Ethernet switch marking the ECN field of IP inside an Ethernet payload.
  • Feed-backward: nodes send congestion signals back toward the lower layer's ingress, as in the ATM Available Bit Rate service.
  • Null: the lower layer cannot become congested except at its IP-aware ingress, so ECN in IP is enough. A point-to-point Ethernet link or a non-blocking fat-tree are examples.
sections.eli5: There are four ways a warning can travel. Pass it forward and up, put it right on the package, send a note back to the start, or do nothing because the road never jams.

sections.title: Marking Only When It Is Safe
sections.content:
For feed-forward-and-up mode, a lower-layer congestion notification system:

  1. SHOULD NOT apply explicit marks to PDUs headed for legacy layer-4 transports that will not understand ECN;
  2. SHOULD NOT mark PDUs if the subnet egress might not propagate the mark upward;
  3. SHOULD be able to tell ECN-PDUs from Not-ECN-PDUs.

A PDU (protocol data unit) is a frame, packet or cell. An ECN-PDU sits on a feedback loop where every node needed to carry the signal back can do so; a Not-ECN-PDU does not. The lower layer need not copy IP's way of telling these apart: labels, tags, flow state or out-of-band signals may do it.

The RFC gives examples. MPLS has no spare header bit, so RFC 5129 requires the operator to upgrade all decapsulating edges of a domain at once when any switch starts marking. TRILL (RFC 9600) marks with a critical ingress-to-egress flag, so an egress that does not understand it drops the frame, which is the desired default. The RFC warns that plug-and-play technologies such as Ethernet need a fail-safe approach rather than careful configuration.
sections.eli5: Only use the warning flag when the person at the end can read it. Otherwise, it is better to just drop the package so the sender gets the message the old way.

sections.title: Encapsulation Guidelines
sections.content:
The subnet ingress (the encapsulator) has three jobs.

First, an egress capability check: it must be sure the egress will propagate any marking added to the outer header. That can be guaranteed by configuration (as in RFC 5129), by the ingress checking the egress, or by a design where a legacy egress treats a marked PDU as invalid and discards it.

Second, if the check fails, the ingress SHOULD disable congestion notification at the lower layer, for example by marking the outer header as a Not-ECN-PDU.

Third, the standard congestion monitoring baseline: once the egress is known to be safe, the ingress SHOULD encode the same congestion level in the outer header as it received, for example by copying it. A node that is not the Load Regulator SHOULD NOT reset outer CE markings to zero. This lets monitoring of outer headers measure congestion along the whole path since the sender. The RFC's example: with 0.4% CE on the outer header and 0.1% on the inner, 0.4% was introduced overall and 0.3% since the current subnet ingress.
sections.eli5: Before putting a warning flag on a parcel, check that the delivery person at the other end will pass it on. If not, do not use the flag. And do not wipe flags that were already there.

sections.title: Decapsulation Guidelines
sections.content:
A subnet egress SHOULD NOT simply copy the congestion notification from the outer header to the forwarded one. It SHOULD work out the outgoing value from the inner and outer headers using the rules below. Earlier rules win over later ones.

  1. If the inner header is a Not-ECN-PDU and the outer carries an explicit congestion mark, drop is the only signal the transport will understand. If the mark is the most severe possible, the packet MUST be dropped; with several severity levels and a lesser mark, SHOULD be dropped. If the outer is unmarked or also Not-ECN, forward it as a Not-ECN-PDU.
  2. If only the outer header lacks ECN support, forward the inner header unchanged.
  3. If congestion is a numeric level, as in QCN control frames, convert it into a frequency of marks in outgoing IP packets.
  4. If the headers carry different severities, forward the more severe one.
  5. For combinations that should not occur, it MAY be appropriate to log and raise an alarm. If a safe outgoing codepoint exists, the PDU SHOULD be forwarded rather than dropped; alarms and policy-mediated drop are preferred over hard-coded drop.
sections.eli5: When unwrapping a parcel, look at both labels. If the receiver cannot read warning flags but one is set, throw the parcel away. Otherwise, keep the more serious of the two warnings.

sections.title: Tunnel Sequences and Reframing
sections.content:
When a packet crosses several identical tunnels in sequence, such as GTP tunnels in 3GPP networks, every step can follow RFC 6040. As an optimization, a node that decapsulates and immediately re-encapsulates MAY copy the incoming outer ECN field to the outgoing outer header and the inner field to the outgoing inner header. Tunnel endpoints SHOULD let the operator configure whether this optimization is enabled, because it lets the whole sequence be monitored as if it were a single tunnel.

Reframing matters only where a pure Layer 2 node marks frames and frame boundaries do not match IP packet boundaries. The decapsulating IP node SHOULD propagate marks from frames to IP packets, and new marks SHOULD propagate immediately. Marking propagation happens before the Not-ECN-PDU drop rule above. If ECN-PDUs and non-ECN-PDUs are mixed into one IP packet, the decapsulation specification SHOULD require it to be discarded. The RFC also sketches a counter scheme: an in counter tracks octets in marked frames and an out counter tracks octets in marked IP packets, and packets are marked while in exceeds out.
sections.eli5: If a parcel goes through several identical wrappings in a row, you can skip some unwrapping steps, as long as the warning still comes out the same. If the wrapping splits parcels differently, the warning should still land on some parcel quickly.

sections.title: Feed-Up-and-Forward and Feed-Backward Guidance
sections.content:
Feed-up-and-forward applies, for example, to IP packets in Ethernet, which has no congestion notification, or to a 3GPP base station whose PDCP layer has none. It looks like a layering violation, but is called a benign optimization when three rules hold. If a built-in lower-layer mechanism exists, mixing is safe, though the built-in one is generally more efficient. The search for the IP header SHOULD be limited, with a fall-back to drop or the built-in mechanism. And the first IP header found is enough, as the tunnel egress can propagate upward later. The RFC notes it is not a general replacement, since link-layer encryption, non-IP payloads, and switches without Layer 3 capability can all get in the way.

For feed-backward mode no detailed guidelines are given. A subnetwork technology meant to interface to IP SHOULD NOT be designed using only feed-backward mode. The RFC notes that ICMP source quench was an early backward approach that fell out of favor and is formally deprecated, partly because spoofing was hard to detect. QCN is confined to scenarios like some data centres.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the switch can peek at the label inside the box and mark it directly, but it should not dig too deep. Sending a note back to the start of the road is slow and easy to fake, so do not rely on it alone.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If a lower-layer protocol gets an in-band congestion field, that field SHOULD be specified as mutable in transit. Otherwise, interior nodes that signal congestion would invalidate any authentication applied to the header.

The RFC also raises signal integrity concerns, such as senders ignoring signals or networks suppressing them. It points to end-to-end approaches like Congestion Exposure (ConEx) and a sender-side test for suppressed signals. Since end-to-end integrity inherently achieves hop-by-hop integrity, it considers it pointless to design hop-by-hop integrity into a new lower-layer protocol. Vulnerability to spoofing is one reason feed-backward mode is deprecated. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: The warning flag must be allowed to change on the way, or the packet's seal would break. And checking that warnings are not hidden is better done from end to end than at every stop.

messages.label: Mark in L2 header
messages.note: Congestion at the switch output queue is marked in the lower-layer header.

messages.label: Mark in L3 (IP) header
messages.note: When the router removes the L2 header it propagates the mark up into IP.

messages.label: Mark fed back in L4 ACK
messages.note: The transport (for example TCP) reports it to the sender.

items.title: Egress capability check
items.text: Be sure the egress will propagate any marking before adding one.

items.title: If the check fails
items.text: Disable congestion notification at the lower layer, for example by marking the PDU as Not-ECN.

items.title: Monitoring baseline
items.text: Copy incoming congestion levels to the outer header and do not reset CE markings to zero.
